claim: Fights for foreigners are arranged by the gym owner or trainer
value: Trainer or gym owner schedules the fight; some gyms receive fight requests weekly and pick fighters who represent the gym well
source_title: Having Your First Muay Thai Fight in Bangkok, Thailand

claim: Typical short fight camp length for a visiting fighter
value: Fight preparation takes at least 3 weeks, ideally 4 weeks (gym requires prior regular training and an amateur fight)
source_title: Muay Thai fights for foreigners in Thailand (Punch it Gym)

claim: Time to become fight-ready for someone who has never competed
value: Two to three months of preparation in Thailand
source_title: Muay Thai professional fighter as a foreigner in Thailand (Punch it Gym)

claim: Training volume recommended before a fight
value: About 20 hours per week (3-4 h/day, 6 days/week) for at least 8 weeks, sparring every second or third day
source_title: Muay Thai Fight in Thailand: 10 Tips to Prepare (Sumalee Boxing Gym)

claim: Prior experience asked by a gym for foreigners fighting there
value: 3-4 Muay Thai or kickboxing sessions per week over several months, 2-3 runs of 4-5 km per week; amateur fight recommended; gym refuses over-40s without sufficient experience
source_title: Muay Thai fights for foreigners in Thailand (Punch it Gym)

claim: Fight frequency limit stated by a gym
value: Cannot fight more than once a month
source_title: Muay Thai professional fighter as a foreigner in Thailand (Punch it Gym)

claim: Foreigners rarely earn a living from fights
value: Gym operator: hardly possible for 90% of foreign fighters; only a few foreigners earn a living, usually sponsored by their gym
source_title: Recap of Our Muay Thai AMA with Frances Watthanaya

claim: Beginner purse range and gym split
value: Purse split 50/50 with the gym; about 3,000-5,000 THB per fight in the first months
source_title: Muay Thai professional fighter as a foreigner in Thailand (Punch it Gym)

claim: Purse example, women's circuit in Chiang Mai
value: Average about 3,000 THB per fight including title bouts, reported as not enough to cover living costs (undated)
source_title: Fighting on Holidays (Muay Thai Citizen)

claim: Top-tier Bangkok stadium purses are far higher than other promotions
value: Lumpinee and Rajadamnern fighters are paid 10 to 15 times more than other promotions; fighting there takes years
source_title: Having Your First Muay Thai Fight in Bangkok, Thailand

claim: Fight format
value: Up to 5 rounds of 3 minutes, 2-minute rests; elbows are legal scoring weapons
source_title: Muay Thai rules (muaythai2000.com / WMC)

claim: Official match length at Thai venues
value: Maximum 5 rounds of up to 3 minutes
source_title: Muay Thai in Thailand: Best Places to Watch Fights

claim: Thai stadium weight class list (illustrative, WMC/stadium style)
value: Mini Flyweight 104 lb, Jr Fly 108, Fly 112 (50.8 kg), Jr Bantam 115, Bantam 118 (53.5 kg), Jr Feather 122, Feather 126 (57.2 kg), Jr Light 130, Light 135 (61.2 kg), Jr Welter 140, Welter 147 (66.7 kg), Jr Middle 154, Middle 160 (71.6 kg), Light Heavy 175 (79.4 kg), Cruiser 190, Heavy over 190
source_title: Muay Thai rules (muaythai2000.com / WMC)

claim: Weight classes differ between promotions
value: Same-named classes can cover very different weights in different promotions; confirm limit with promoter. Elite Thai list closely tied to Lumpinee/Rajadamnern and WBC Muay Thai
source_title: Muay Thai Weight Classes (Muay Thai Citizen)

claim: Weigh-in timing and weight-cut realism
value: Weigh-ins are the day before or the morning of the fight (about 12-24 h to rehydrate); a missed weight can cancel the fight or be accepted by promoter and opponent; dehydration risks can be severe
source_title: Muay Thai Weight Classes (Muay Thai Citizen)

claim: Weight rules vary by promotion in Bangkok
value: Super Muay Thai requires being within stated class; Asiatique may not require a weigh-in or reveal opponent weight until fight day
source_title: Having Your First Muay Thai Fight in Bangkok, Thailand

claim: Pre-fight medical in rulebook (WMC)
value: Ringside physician examines all fighters before weigh-in and after the fight; mandatory rest after a bout: 7, 14, 21 days or 30 days after a KO loss
source_title: Muay Thai rules (muaythai2000.com / WMC)

claim: Medical check in practice (anecdote)
value: A foreign fighter reports being taken to the doctor on arrival at the venue for a blood pressure check, described as the norm; no official Thai document found on foreigner requirements
source_title: Seventy-Seventh Fight (8 Limbs US)

claim: Minimum fighter age and referee rules in WMC rulebook
value: Minimum fighter age 14 and 100 lb; referee primary duty is to safeguard fighters; can stop mismatch bouts; official gloves supplied by organizers (8 oz up to 122 lb, 10 oz above to 147 lb)
source_title: Muay Thai rules (muaythai2000.com / WMC)

claim: Thai law governing professional Muay Thai
value: Boxing Act B.E. 2542 (1999) regulates promotion, protection, control of professional boxing and Muay Thai; Sports Authority of Thailand and its Boxing Board of Control oversee rules; registration and medical sections not verified in this research
source_title: Boxing Act B.E. 2542 (muaythai2000.com)

claim: Work permit status for professional foreign fighters
value: Two conflicting positions: (a) no work permit category exists for pro fighters, grey area, fighters keep tourist visas up to date; (b) paid fighting income means DTV is not usable and a Non-B visa plus work permit via a sponsoring Thai organization (2,000,000 THB capital, 4:1 Thai ratio) is needed. Not resolved by an official source
source_title: Thailand Visa for Professional Athletes (Issa Compass)

claim: Grey area view on work permits
value: "There is no work permit yet available for professional fighters, it remains a grey area"; some gyms offer education visas
source_title: Recap of Our Muay Thai AMA with Frances Watthanaya

claim: DTV covers Muay Thai training (soft power)
value: Muay Thai training with enrolment letter qualifies; 500,000 THB financial proof (or sponsorship letter per some embassies); 180 days per entry, extendable once; apply from outside Thailand via e-visa
source_title: Thailand DTV visa 2026: requirements, cost and how to apply (Thaiger)

claim: DTV and paid fights
value: One guide says earning income from fighting excludes the DTV and requires cancelling it; unconfirmed by an official source, check with embassy or lawyer
source_title: Thailand Visa for Professional Athletes (Issa Compass)

claim: Travel insurance often excludes combat sports
value: World Nomads: training only covered, martial arts competitions or bouts listed among exclusions; SafetyWing: Muay Thai and martial arts excluded unless adventure add-on; confirm in writing
source_title: World Nomads Review (Thailand Starter Kit)

claim: Fight insurance advice from fighters
value: Many companies exclude martial arts; specialist muay thai training/fighting cover exists (SportsCoverDirect, availability depends on country); stitches and hospital care are relatively cheap locally
source_title: Fighting in Thailand: insurance (8 Limbs forum)

claim: Chiang Mai venues
value: Thapae Boxing Stadium: 9-11:30 pm, closed Sundays per one guide, 400-600 THB; Loi Kroh Stadium: fights 9:30 pm-midnight, 400 THB, typically westerners against Thai boxers; Chiang Mai Boxing Stadium: professional cards, about 600 THB cheapest; Kalare not documented
source_title: Where to go to watch boxing in Chiang Mai (Chiang Mai CityLife)

claim: Thapae stadium mixes foreigners and Thais
value: Fights are typically between westerners and Thai boxers, women and men (travel listing, promotional)
source_title: Thapae Boxing Stadium (Visit Thailand Today)

claim: Bangkok stadium picture
value: Rajadamnern is the oldest, nightly events, tickets from 1,500 THB; Lumpinee is run by the Thai Army, events Friday and Saturday, from 800 THB; most pro Thai fighters compete there and access takes years
source_title: Muay Thai in Thailand: Best Places to Watch Fights

claim: Bangkok entry-level promotions open to foreigners
value: Asiatique (daily except Monday, entry level), Super Muay Thai (Rangsit), True4U (Rangsit), MX Muay Extreme (Asoke); some pair under-10-fight foreigners with 100-fight Thais
source_title: Having Your First Muay Thai Fight in Bangkok, Thailand

claim: Cost of camp training for context
value: Training about 250-400 USD per month, accommodation 200-350 USD at foreigner-friendly gyms (Khao Lak, undated)
source_title: Fighting Muay Thai in Thailand as a Foreigner (We Seek Travel)
